section.title: The Northern Tribes
section.sectionRationale: The Chronicler moves quickly through Issachar, a partial record of Benjamin, a single verse for Naphtali, Manasseh east and west of the Jordan, Ephraim, including the sudden death of two of his sons and the grief-born birth of Beriah, and finally Asher, closing the survey of the tribes descended from Jacob's sons other than Levi and Judah.
section.thesis: By recording, however briefly, every one of the remaining northern tribes, even pausing over Ephraim's raw grief and the small mercy of Beriah's birth, the Chronicler shows the returned exiles that no tribe, however scattered by war and exile of its own, has fallen outside the record of a God who remembers every family descended from Israel.
section.frameNote: Six movements: the descendants of Issachar; the descendants of Benjamin; the descendants of Naphtali; the descendants of Manasseh; Ephraim's grief and the birth of Beriah; and the descendants of Asher.

units.label: The descendants of Issachar
units.note: mighty men of valor, numbered by the thousands

verses.text: The sons of Issachar: Tola, Puah, Jashub, and Shimron, four in all.

The sons of Tola: Uzzi, Rephaiah, Jeriel, Jahmai, Ibsam, and Shemuel, the heads of their {{mishpachah|families}}. In the days of David, 22,600 descendants of Tola were numbered in their genealogies as {{gibbor|mighty men of valor}}.
The son of Uzzi: Izrahiah. The sons of Izrahiah: Michael, Obadiah, Joel, and Isshiah. All five of them were chiefs.
In addition to them, according to their genealogy, they had 36,000 troops for battle, for they had many wives and children.
Their kinsmen belonging to all the families of Issachar who were mighty men of valor totaled 87,000, as listed in their genealogies.

units.label: The descendants of Benjamin
units.note: a partial record of a large tribe

verses.text: The three sons of Benjamin: Bela, Becher, and Jediael.
The sons of Bela: Ezbon, Uzzi, Uzziel, Jerimoth, and Iri, heads of their families, five in all. There were 22,034 mighty men of valor listed in their genealogies.
The sons of Becher: Zemirah, Joash, Eliezer, Elioenai, Omri, Jeremoth, Abijah, Anathoth, and Alemeth; all these were Becher's sons.
Their genealogies were recorded according to the heads of their families, 20,200 mighty men of valor.
The son of Jediael: Bilhan. The sons of Bilhan: Jeush, Benjamin, Ehud, Chenaanah, Zethan, Tarshish, and Ahishahar.
All these sons of Jediael were heads of their families, mighty men of valor; there were 17,200 fit for battle.
The Shuppites and Huppites were descendants of Ir, and the Hushites were descendants of Aher.

units.label: The descendants of Naphtali
units.note: one verse for a whole tribe

verses.text: The sons of Naphtali: Jahziel, Guni, Jezer, and Shallum, the descendants of Bilhah.

units.label: The descendants of Manasseh
units.note: east of the Jordan, in Gilead

verses.text: The descendants of Manasseh: Asriel through his Aramean concubine. She also gave birth to Machir the father of Gilead.
Machir took a wife from among the Huppites and Shuppites. The name of his sister was Maacah. Another descendant was named Zelophehad, who had only daughters.
Machir's wife Maacah gave birth to a son, and she named him Peresh. His brother was named Sheresh, and his sons were Ulam and Rekem.
The son of Ulam: Bedan. These were the sons of Gilead son of Machir, the son of Manasseh.
His sister Hammolecheth gave birth to Ishhod, Abiezer, and Mahlah.
And these were the sons of Shemida: Ahian, Shechem, Likhi, and Aniam.

units.label: Ephraim's grief and the birth of Beriah
units.note: sons killed stealing livestock, and a son born in tragedy

verses.text: The descendants of Ephraim: Shuthelah, Bered his son, Tahath his son, Eleadah his son, Tahath his son,
Zabad his son, and Shuthelah his son. Ezer and Elead were killed by the natives of Gath, because they went down to steal their livestock.
Their father Ephraim {{avel|mourned}} for many days, and his relatives came to comfort him.
And again he slept with his wife, and she conceived and gave birth to a son. So he {{shem|named}} him Beriah, because tragedy had come upon his house.
His daughter was Sheerah, who built Lower and Upper Beth-horon, as well as Uzzen-sheerah.
Additionally, Rephah was his son, Resheph his son, Telah his son, Tahan his son,
Ladan his son, Ammihud his son, Elishama his son,
Nun his son, and Joshua his son.
Their holdings and settlements included Bethel and its villages, Naaran to the east, Gezer and its villages to the west, and Shechem and its villages as far as Ayyah and its villages.
And along the borders of Manasseh were Beth-shean, Taanach, Megiddo, and Dor, together with their villages. The descendants of Joseph son of Israel lived in these towns.

units.label: The descendants of Asher
units.note: choice and mighty men, chiefs among the leaders

verses.text: The children of Asher: Imnah, Ishvah, Ishvi, Beriah, and their sister Serah.
The sons of Beriah: Heber, as well as Malchiel, who was the father of Birzaith.
Heber was the father of Japhlet, Shomer, and Hotham, and of their sister Shua.
The sons of Japhlet: Pasach, Bimhal, and Ashvath. These were Japhlet's sons.
The sons of Shemer: Ahi, Rohgah, Hubbah, and Aram.
The sons of his brother Helem: Zophah, Imna, Shelesh, and Amal.
The sons of Zophah: Suah, Harnepher, Shual, Beri, Imrah,
Bezer, Hod, Shamma, Shilshah, Ithran, and Beera.
The sons of Jether: Jephunneh, Pispa, and Ara.
The sons of Ulla: Arah, Hanniel, and Rizia.

All these were the descendants of Asher, heads of their families, choice and mighty men of valor, and chiefs among the leaders. The number of men fit for battle, recorded in their genealogies, was 26,000.

mishpachah.gloss: Clan or extended family. Even Issachar, a tribe rarely mentioned elsewhere in Scripture, has its heads of families and thousands of warriors carefully recorded, showing that every mishpachah within Israel, however minor its later reputation, mattered enough to be counted and named.

gibbor.gloss: Mighty man of valor, a warrior of strength and standing. The phrase recurs like a refrain across this chapter, for Issachar, Benjamin, and Asher alike, a repeated reminder that these lesser-known tribes were nonetheless real and formidable, contributing real strength to Israel's defense even though their stories are rarely told elsewhere.

avel.gloss: To mourn, to grieve. Ephraim mourned for many days after his sons Ezer and Elead were killed, and his relatives came to comfort him, an unusually personal and emotional moment inside an otherwise dry genealogical record, showing that even ancient family trees are made of real grief and real loss.

shem.gloss: Name. Ephraim named his newborn son Beriah, a name the BSB footnote explains sounds like the Hebrew word for tragedy or disaster, so that every time the name was spoken it carried the memory of the sons lost and the grief that preceded the child's birth, a naming that turned sorrow itself into a permanent, spoken memorial.

basic.context: This chapter moves briskly through several tribes that receive little space elsewhere in the Bible: Issachar, with tens of thousands of warriors listed by genealogy; a partial record of Benjamin's sons (a fuller account of Benjamin follows in chapter 8); a single verse for all of Naphtali; the descendants of Manasseh who settled in Gilead; Ephraim, whose record pauses for real, personal tragedy, the deaths of two sons killed while raiding livestock, his father's extended mourning, and the birth of another son named Beriah, a name recalling that very tragedy; and finally Asher, closing with a substantial list of warriors and chiefs. A reader naturally asks why some tribes get so little space compared to Judah or Levi, and why the story stops, however briefly, to dwell on Ephraim's grief in the middle of a long list of names.
basic.hermeneutics: This is genealogical record punctuated once, briefly but movingly, by real narrative: Ephraim's loss and the birth of Beriah (7:20-23). The uneven space given to each tribe, one verse for Naphtali, ten for Manasseh, ten for Ephraim, is not a statement about which tribes mattered to God, since even the shortest entries record real names before Him; rather, it likely reflects how much genealogical material had survived and was available to the Chronicler by the time of writing, centuries after the tribal allotments themselves.
basic.originalLanguages: The chapter is threaded with mishpachah, clan, groupings and repeated tallies of gibbor chayil, mighty men of valor, a phrase that recurs for Issachar, Benjamin, and Asher alike, insisting that these lesser-known tribes were nonetheless strong and real. At its emotional center, Ephraim's avel, mourning, for his slain sons is recorded with unusual tenderness, and the shem, name, he gives his next son, Beriah, meaning tragedy, turns grief itself into a spoken, lasting memorial rather than something hidden or forgotten.
basic.typology: Ephraim's grief, followed by the birth of a son whose very name recalls the tragedy that preceded him, anticipates the pattern seen throughout Scripture of sorrow giving way, in God's timing, to new life and new hope, a pattern that finds its fullest expression in the sorrow of the cross giving way to the joy of the resurrection.
basic.christ: Though this chapter's names rarely reappear later in Scripture, Joshua, listed here in Ephraim's line (7:27) as the son of Nun, is the very Joshua who led Israel into the promised land, himself a namesake and forerunner of Jesus, since Joshua and Jesus share the same underlying Hebrew name, Yehoshua, meaning the LORD saves. Ephraim's mourning followed by a son whose name carries the memory of tragedy also points toward the pattern the gospel completes: real, named grief that does not go unacknowledged, met at last by God's own greater answer to sorrow in the resurrection of Christ.
basic.god: God is shown here as a God who records real grief alongside real genealogy: Ephraim's mourning for his sons is not glossed over or skipped past but is written into Israel's sacred record with the same care given to any king's lineage. This is a God who does not merely count names abstractly but attends to the sorrow and loss woven through ordinary family histories, and who allows even a name born from tragedy, Beriah, to carry forward into the ongoing story of His people.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 46:20-25 provides the earlier record of the sons of Ephraim, Manasseh, Naphtali, and Asher that this chapter expands. Numbers 26 gives a wilderness-era census of these same tribes. Matthew 1:1 and Acts 7:45 identify Joshua, named in this chapter's line of Ephraim, as bearing the same name later given to Jesus, both meaning the LORD saves.
basic.oneStory: Even the tribes that receive the least space in Scripture, Issachar, Naphtali, and the rest, are recorded here with real names, real warriors, and, in Ephraim's case, real and personal grief. For a community returned from exile, uncertain which tribes and families still had any place in Israel's story, this chapter's insistence on remembering every tribe, however briefly, however painfully, is a small but real assurance that no part of God's people, and no sorrow they carried, falls outside His notice, a notice fulfilled at last in Christ, who bears every sorrow and completes every broken family's hope.

context.literary:
The chapter's uneven proportions are themselves a structural argument. Naphtali collapses to a single verse, four names and nothing more, while Manasseh, Ephraim, and Asher each receive roughly ten, an imbalance so pronounced that a first time reader might suspect an accident of transmission rather than deliberate design; yet placed where it is, directly after the extensive treatments of Simeon, Reuben, Gad, and Levi, and just before Benjamin receives an entire chapter to itself, the unevenness reads less like carelessness and more like the Chronicler working with whatever material survived a nation's scattering, and refusing to let a thin record become no record at all.

Ephraim's unit, verses 20 to 29, breaks the chapter's list making rhythm with genuine narrative, cause, "Ezer and Elead were killed by the natives of Gath," response, "mourned for many days," and resolution, a son born and named for the very tragedy that preceded him. Positioned almost exactly at the midpoint of the nine chapters of genealogy that open this book, that pause functions as an interpretive key for everything around it: every bare name on either side of this story represents a family capable of exactly this kind of loss.

The chapter's final verse, tallying Asher's 26,000 fighting men, closes on the same military note that opened the chapter with Issachar's 87,000, so the whole unit is framed, deliberately, by numbers, real strength on either end bracketing one family's very real grief in the middle.
context.historical:
By the time Chronicles reached its final written form, every tribe named in this chapter except the Transjordan remnant already covered in chapter 5 had been carried off in the Assyrian deportations that followed 722 BC, more than a century before the Chronicler's own post-exilic audience read these lists. Recording Issachar's, Naphtali's, Manasseh's, Ephraim's, and Asher's family lines here was therefore an act of memory rather than administration, since none of these tribes could supply the Chronicler with a living, organized community to consult the way Judah, Levi, and Benjamin still could.

Ephraim's tragedy fits a known pattern of border raiding between Israelite settlers and Philistine cities; Gath lay close enough to Ephraimite territory that livestock theft across that boundary, met with lethal reprisal, was a real and recurring danger long before Goliath made Gath famous in David's own generation. The size of the armies recorded, Issachar's 87,000, Benjamin's tens of thousands in the next chapter, likely reflect musters taken at different points across the monarchy rather than one simultaneous census, since Israel's total population could not have sustained every tribal figure in these chapters standing under arms at once; the Chronicler preserved whatever numbers his sources gave him for each tribe's own moment of record. Manasseh's Aramean concubine, verse 14, and its Gileadite branch east of the Jordan reflect the same pattern of intermarriage with surrounding peoples already visible in Judah's genealogy in chapter 2, a normal feature of tribal life in Canaan's mixed population rather than an isolated scandal.
context.canonical:
This chapter completes a roll call Genesis began at Jacob's deathbed and in Egypt: Naphtali, Manasseh, Ephraim, and Asher all appear already among the sons listed in Genesis 46:20-25, and Jacob's own oracles over several of them, Issachar a strong donkey content to serve for good land, Genesis 49:14-15, Asher's rich food fit for royalty, Genesis 49:20, are the same tribal character sketches this chapter's bare genealogies quietly assume without repeating. Numbers 26:28-51 supplies a wilderness census of these same names one generation earlier, so that Chronicles and Numbers together trace an unbroken thread from the exodus generation to the settled tribes centuries later.

Joshua's account of Manasseh's daughters, Zelophehad's line among them, receiving "an inheritance among their father's brothers... in keeping with the command of the LORD," Joshua 17:3-6, stands directly behind the unusual mention here of Zelophehad "who had only daughters," verse 15, confirming that this chapter's genealogy still honors, generations later, a legal ruling first settled in Numbers 27:1-7. And Joshua himself, named in Ephraim's line at verse 27, ties this whole chapter back to the conquest narrative that made these tribal territories possible in the first place, since it was an Ephraimite who led Israel into the very land these families are recorded as inhabiting.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The Chronicler intended his readers to recognize that God's people extend further than the two tribes, Judah and Benjamin, who could actually be counted in the returned community. By recording Issachar, Naphtali, Manasseh, Ephraim, and Asher, tribes with no living representatives the author could interview, no cities his own generation still occupied, he insists that "all Israel," a phrase this book uses repeatedly, has never meant only the visible remnant currently in Jerusalem.

He also intended, through the single sustained narrative interruption about Ephraim, to teach his readers how to read every other name in these nine chapters: not as abstract data but as compressed family history, capable of the same grief, the same loss, and the same quiet perseverance his own generation had just lived through. A community that had itself buried children and rebuilt afterward needed to see that kind of loss written into Scripture's own family record, not edited out of it for the sake of tidiness.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter records specific musters, specific deaths, and one specific act of mourning; it prescribes no method of grieving, no minimum length of mourning, no formula for naming children after tragedy. Ephraim's example is not a command to name every child born after loss for that loss, only a recorded instance of one father's honesty about his own grief, an honesty the text neither commends nor criticizes but simply preserves.

Likewise, the wildly uneven space given to each tribe describes what records survived, not a ranking of which tribes God valued most; readers should resist mining this chapter for a principle about proportional divine attention and instead take from it the simpler, sturdier truth that grief belongs inside the record of faith rather than outside it, and that even a single verse can hold a real family before God.

debates.question: Why does Ephraim's personal tragedy (7:20-23) receive extended narrative treatment while most other tribes in this chapter receive only bare lists of names?

views.label: The Chronicler preserved an available, striking family tradition
views.case: It is likely that this particular story survived in Israel's collective memory or written sources with unusual vividness, perhaps because Ephraim was Joseph's son and a leading northern tribe, and the Chronicler, working from whatever records he had, simply included what had been preserved rather than omitting a moving, well-known episode.

views.label: The story functions deliberately to humanize the whole genealogical section
views.case: Placed roughly at the midpoint of the long genealogies spanning chapters 1 through 9, this rare narrative pause reminds readers that every name in every list represents a real family with real losses, joys, and griefs, not merely data; it functions as an interpretive key inviting readers to feel the human weight behind even the driest lists surrounding it.

debates.bearing: Both readings agree the passage is a deliberate, meaningful inclusion rather than filler, and both invite readers to recognize the real human lives, complete with real sorrow, behind every name recorded in these opening chapters.

debates.question: What should Christians take from long, uneven genealogies like this one, where some tribes receive many verses and others almost none?

views.label: A lesson in the danger of comparing our significance to others
views.case: If even a whole tribe of Israel could be reduced to a single verse (7:13) without thereby mattering less to God, believers should resist measuring their own worth or calling by how much attention or recognition they receive compared to others; faithfulness, not visibility, is what God records and values.

views.label: A lesson in trusting God's larger, often hidden, purposes
views.case: The unevenness reflects incomplete historical records rather than divine favoritism; readers are reminded that Scripture itself does not claim to give a complete account of every person's story, and that God's care for those whose stories are barely told, like Naphtali here, is no less real for being undocumented in detail.

debates.bearing: Both lessons converge on the same pastoral point: a life recorded in only a line, or in no line at all that others can see, is not therefore unseen or unvalued by God, who kept perfect account of every tribe named in this chapter, however briefly.

study.originalLanguages:
Beyond mishpachah, gibbor chayil, avel, and shem already introduced, the word behind "concubine" in verse 14, pilegesh, deserves a note of its own. It describes a genuine wife of secondary status, not a casual arrangement, whose children carried real inheritance rights, as Machir's own descent through this very concubine shows; the word appears for Jacob's own concubines Bilhah and Zilpah, Genesis 35:22, and later for Gideon's Shechem born son Abimelech, Judges 8:31, always marking a socially recognized, if unequal, family bond rather than an illegitimate one.

Gibbor chayil, mighty of valor, recurs for Issachar, verse 2, Benjamin in the next chapter, and Asher at this chapter's close, verse 40, a formula built from gibbor, strong, and chayil, which can mean physical strength, an army, or moral substance depending on context, the same word describing the virtuous wife of Proverbs 31:10; Chronicles likely intends the full range at once here, these were tribes of genuine, all around substance, not merely large armies.

Avel, to mourn, is a strong verb of visible, often ritual grief, the same word used for Jacob's inconsolable mourning over Joseph, Genesis 37:34-35, and for the entire nation's response to Aaron's death, Numbers 20:29; applying it to Ephraim without qualification places his private sorrow in the same register Scripture reserves for its most significant public losses, a signal that this family's grief mattered as much, on its own smaller scale, as a nation's.

Shem, name, carries weight throughout Hebrew narrative that English names rarely do, since a Hebrew name typically states a claim or a memory rather than merely labeling a person; Beriah, in tragedy, joins a small company of names built the same way, Ichabod, the glory has departed, 1 Samuel 4:21, and Jabez, he caused pain, 1 Chronicles 4:9, each one a family's decision to keep a hard truth spoken aloud in every generation that used the name, rather than letting time quietly erase it.

Finally, the phrase "chiefs among the leaders" for Asher in verse 40 stacks overlapping words for prominence, gibbor and rosh, mighty and chief, an unusually dense pile of honorifics for a tribe otherwise almost invisible elsewhere in Scripture, as if the Chronicler wanted no reader to conclude that thin coverage elsewhere meant thin substance here.

Even the chapter's opening count, verse 5's tally of Issachar's warriors "as listed in their genealogies," uses the same yachas root Chronicles leans on across all nine chapters, formal enrollment rather than casual estimate, a reminder that these numbers, however large, were never meant as rounded guesses but as figures some scribe once actually verified name by name.

typology.type: Joshua, of Ephraim's line, who led Israel into the promised land
typology.fulfillment: Joshua's Hebrew name, Yehoshua, means the LORD saves, the identical name later given to Jesus, and his conquest, real and complete as Joshua himself testifies, not one word of all the LORD's good promises having failed, Joshua 21:45, still left Israel in a land where wars, exile, and grief like Ephraim's own remained possible. Hebrews 4:8-9 draws the necessary conclusion, if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken later about another day, so the very completeness of Joshua's conquest is what proves a greater rest, and a greater namesake, was always still to come.

typology.type: Ephraim's grief giving way to a son who carried the family forward
typology.fulfillment: Beriah's birth did not erase Ezer and Elead's deaths; his very name kept them present in every generation that spoke it. John 16:20-22 promises believers exactly this kind of grief transformed rather than denied, you will grieve, but your grief will turn to joy, and no one will take that joy away, language that does not ask sorrow to disappear but promises it will finally be outlasted, precisely what Ephraim's household could only hope for in one child's birth.

typology.type: Scattered tribes, some reduced to a single verse, still named and recorded
typology.fulfillment: Naphtali's one verse and Asher's ten stand together in the same chapter without comment on the disparity, as though the length of the record were never the point, only its existence. Revelation 7:9's great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, tribe, people, and tongue, answers that same disparity on the largest possible scale, a gathering where Naphtali's descendants, however thin their earthly record, stand named and complete before the very throne this genealogy's compilers could only anticipate from a distance.

study.christ:
Tucked without fanfare into Ephraim's line is a name the Gospels will make famous: "Nun his son, and Joshua his son," verse 27, the same Joshua who succeeded Moses. His Hebrew name, Yehoshua, is the identical name later given to Jesus, Matthew 1:21 explaining that He would be so named "because He will save His people from their sins," so that centuries before the incarnation, an Ephraimite family record already carried, unknowingly, the very name the world's rescuer would bear.

Joshua led Israel into a real, physical rest, yet Hebrews 4:8 insists that rest was never final, "if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken later about another day," pointing past the conquest this chapter's tribes actually occupy to "a Sabbath rest" still remaining, Hebrews 4:9, for the people of God. Where Joshua's rest still left room for Philistine raids, buried sons, and a father's extended mourning, the very grief this chapter records in Ephraim's household, the greater Joshua's rest promises an end to exactly that kind of loss, Revelation 21:4's "no more death or mourning or crying or pain."

Ephraim's own story supplies Christ by pattern rather than by name. Real death, verse 21, met by real, extended grief, verse 22, "mourned for many days," met at last by new life that does not erase the loss but carries its memory forward in Beriah's very name, verse 23, is the shape of the gospel itself compressed into nine verses: the cross is not skipped past on the way to the resurrection, and the resurrection does not pretend the cross never happened. Jesus, after rising, still carried the wounds of His own death, John 20:27, exactly as Beriah's name carried forward the memory of Ephraim's.

And the chapter's larger pattern, tribes scattered by conquest and exile, some reduced to almost nothing on the page, still faithfully recorded rather than quietly dropped, anticipates the fuller gathering Christ Himself promises, "other sheep that are not of this fold... I must bring them also," John 10:16, a shepherd who loses none of His scattered flock, unlike the tribes this chapter can only partially trace, however carefully it tries.
study.god:
God is shown here as attentive to scale in both directions at once, numbering Issachar's 87,000 fighting men in the same breath as recording a single father's grief over two sons, without treating the smaller number as less significant than the larger. Nothing in the text suggests He measures a family's worth by the length of its genealogy; Naphtali's single verse sits inside the same inspired record as Asher's ten, both equally preserved, both equally real before Him.

He is present in Ephraim's mourning not by removing the grief but by allowing comfort to arrive through ordinary means, "his relatives came to comfort him," verse 22, a detail the text records as simply as it records any birth or death elsewhere in the list; God's care here looks like family showing up rather than like a miracle intervening, an entirely ordinary form of grace easy to miss inside a genealogy.

He is also the God who lets painful memory stand rather than smoothing it away. Nothing in the text required Ephraim to name his son after tragedy; he could have chosen any name at all, yet the record preserves his choice to keep the loss spoken rather than buried, and God's own Scripture preserves that choice permanently, an implicit endorsement of honest remembering over polished forgetting.

He is faithful across scattering. Every tribe in this chapter had already been carried off by Assyria before the Chronicler wrote, yet He had not allowed their family identities to vanish entirely; someone, somewhere, still held records detailed enough for Issachar's chiefs, Manasseh's daughters' names, and Asher's genealogy to reach the Chronicler's hand, evidence of a providence operating quietly underneath a scattering that looked, on the surface, like total loss.

And He is the God who let an Ephraimite lead Israel into the land in the first place, verse 27, choosing His human instruments from ordinary tribal lines rather than from any single privileged family, a pattern that continues when the ultimate deliverer bearing Joshua's own name comes not from Ephraim's line at all but from Judah's, already traced earlier in this book, God working out one promise through many different tribes rather than concentrating every good gift in a single family.

crossReferences.note: This earlier list already names Ephraim, Manasseh, Naphtali, and the sons of Bilhah among those who went down to Egypt with Jacob, a small handful of persons in all. What Chronicles records here as tribes numbering tens of thousands began, within living memory of Genesis, as a few named individuals in one family migrating for survival.

The wilderness census counts these same tribes one generation after the exodus, Manasseh and Ephraim together far smaller than the totals recorded here for Issachar and Asher, a difference Chronicles' own later figures continue to reflect across the tribes' subsequent, uneven history of growth.

Jacob's blessing already sketches Issachar as a tribe content to labor for good land rather than to rule, and Asher's food as fit for royalty, character sketches this chapter's bare lists of names and numbers never restate yet clearly assume, since Issachar appears here as a populous, settled tribe and Asher's leaders are called choice men.

Zelophehad's five daughters first petition Moses directly, why should the name of our father disappear from his clan because he had no sons, and the LORD rules in their favor. Their names reappear in Manasseh's own family record here, verse 15, an ordinary genealogical mention that only makes sense against this earlier, deliberately preserved legal victory.

Joshua personally grants Zelophehad's daughters an inheritance among their father's brothers, in keeping with the command of the LORD, language that confirms Numbers' ruling was actually carried out on the ground, not merely legislated. This chapter's casual mention of Zelophehad who had only daughters rests on that earlier, hard won settlement.

Deborah's song remembers Gilead, the very territory Manasseh occupies east of the Jordan in this chapter, remaining beyond the river rather than joining Israel's battle, a much earlier note of the same eastern tribes' uneven commitment already visible in the parallel Reuben material of the previous chapter.

Among David's supporters were men of Issachar who understood the times and knew what Israel should do, a tribe otherwise summed up here only by its numbers. The genealogy's bare figures in verses 1 to 5 hide a discernment the rest of Scripture credits to this same tribe elsewhere.

Joshua's own name in Ephraim's line, verse 27, is the reason Hebrews can argue as it does: if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken later about another day, so a Sabbath rest remains for the people of God. The conquest this chapter's tribes actually possessed was real yet provisional, a down payment on a rest still to come.

Jesus promises His disciples that their grief will turn to joy and that no one will take that joy away, language that answers, on a far larger scale, the exact movement of Ephraim's household from mourning to a son born in hope, sorrow acknowledged honestly rather than denied, then genuinely overtaken by what follows it.

John sees a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, tribe, people, and tongue, standing before the throne, the ultimate answer to a chapter where some tribes survive in ten verses and others in one, since every name this chapter could barely record finds its place there in full.

study.oneStory:
Every tribe named here had already vanished as a functioning, land holding community by the time these words reached their final written form, carried off by Assyria more than a century before the Chronicler's own audience returned from a different captivity in Babylon. That the Chronicler bothered to record them at all, Naphtali reduced to four names in a single verse, Issachar's tens of thousands of warriors, Ephraim's private grief, is itself a small act of resistance against forgetting, proof that being scattered is not the same as being erased from God's own record.

The pattern beneath Ephraim's story, real loss honestly grieved, then new life that carries the memory forward rather than pretending it away, sits at the center of the whole Bible's larger movement from the fall's first real grief to the new creation's promise that grief itself will finally end. Genesis had already given several of these tribes their character in Jacob's deathbed oracles; this chapter shows those characters still recognizably at work generations later, Issachar still bent to labor, Asher's leaders still called choice men, proof that God's earliest words over a family keep shaping its story long after the family itself has scattered.

And buried inside Ephraim's own genealogy is the one name that ties this whole scattered chapter to the story's ultimate resolution: Joshua, whose conquest brought real but incomplete rest, and whose very name, the LORD saves, God would one day give in full to a greater deliverer from a different tribe altogether. The chapter that seems, on its surface, to be this book's thinnest and most forgettable stretch of genealogy turns out to be carrying, inside one family's line, the name of the One who will finally gather every scattered tribe, Naphtali and Asher included, into the single innumerable multitude no exile can touch again.

quiz.q: What is unusual about the space this chapter gives to Naphtali compared to Ephraim or Manasseh?

options.text: Naphtali receives only a single verse, while Manasseh and Ephraim each receive about ten, an unevenness likely reflecting available records rather than differing divine favor.
options.note: Verse 13 gives Naphtali's entire genealogy in one line, in sharp contrast to the fuller treatment of neighboring tribes.

options.text: All the tribes in this chapter receive exactly equal space.
options.note: The chapter is markedly uneven, from one verse for Naphtali to about ten each for Manasseh, Ephraim, and Asher.

options.text: Naphtali is omitted from the chapter entirely.
options.note: Naphtali is named and given a full verse listing four sons, not omitted.

options.text: Naphtali receives more space than any other tribe in the chapter.
options.note: The opposite is true; Naphtali receives the least space of any tribe named in the chapter.

quiz.q: What tragedy struck Ephraim's family, and how did he respond?

options.text: His sons Ezer and Elead were killed while stealing livestock from the natives of Gath, and Ephraim mourned for many days before his relatives came to comfort him.
options.note: Verses 21-22 record both the deaths and Ephraim's extended mourning.

options.text: His sons died of illness, and Ephraim refused to be comforted by anyone.
options.note: The cause of death was violence during a raid, and the text specifically notes his relatives came to comfort him.

options.text: His sons were killed, though the text gives no indication of his emotional response.
options.note: The text explicitly and movingly records his mourning, a rare emotional note within the genealogies.

options.text: His sons were killed in a battle Ephraim himself led against Gath.
options.note: The text specifies they were killed while trying to steal livestock, not in a battle Ephraim led.

quiz.q: Why did Ephraim name his next son Beriah?

options.text: Because tragedy had come upon his house, the name itself carrying the memory of his sons' deaths.
options.note: Verse 23 and the BSB footnote explain that Beriah sounds like the Hebrew word for tragedy or disaster.

options.text: Because Beriah means joy, celebrating the birth as leaving all sorrow behind.
options.note: The name's meaning is tied to tragedy, not joy, deliberately preserving the memory of what had happened.

options.text: Because it was simply a common name in his clan with no particular significance.
options.note: The text explicitly ties the name to the specific tragedy that preceded the birth.

options.text: Because Ephraim wished to honor his deceased sons' memory, though the text does not explain the name's meaning.
options.note: The text does explain the name's meaning directly, tying it to the household's tragedy, which this option denies.

quiz.q: Which notable biblical figure appears in the genealogy of Ephraim in this chapter?

options.text: Joshua, listed as the son of Nun, the very Joshua who later led Israel into the promised land.
options.note: Verse 27 names 'Nun his son, and Joshua his son,' identifying Joshua's place in Ephraim's line.

options.text: Moses, listed as a descendant of Ephraim.
options.note: Moses belonged to the tribe of Levi, not Ephraim; Joshua is the notable figure named here.

options.text: David, listed among Ephraim's descendants.
options.note: David belonged to the tribe of Judah, already covered in a previous section, not Ephraim.

options.text: A leader named Joshua, though the text does not identify him further.
options.note: The context, coming from Ephraim's line through Nun, clearly identifies him as the well-known successor of Moses.

quiz.q: What is the overall theological effect of this chapter's uneven, sometimes very brief, tribal records?

options.text: It shows that every tribe descended from Israel, however scattered or briefly recorded, still has a place in God's record and story.
options.note: Even the single verse given to Naphtali still preserves real names before God, part of the chapter's larger point.

options.text: It proves that only the tribes given the most verses actually mattered to God.
options.note: The chapter's inclusion of even a single verse for Naphtali argues against measuring worth by space given.

options.text: It shows the Chronicler considered these tribes unimportant and included them reluctantly.
options.note: The careful, honest inclusion of even minor details, including Ephraim's grief, argues against reluctance or dismissal.

options.text: It records the tribes accurately, though without any larger theological point being made.
options.note: Given the book's larger purpose of assuring 'all Israel' of their place in God's ongoing story, the varying space is not without theological significance.

questions: Naphtali is summed up in a single verse, yet still recorded by name before God. Where in your life do you feel like you receive less attention or recognition than others, and how does this passage reassure you that God's record of you is not measured the same way?
Ephraim's grief over his sons is recorded honestly, without being smoothed over or hidden. What grief are you carrying that you have not yet allowed others, or God, to see and comfort?

Ephraim named his next son after the very tragedy his family had suffered, refusing to erase the memory even in a moment of new life. How might naming your own pain honestly, rather than pretending it away, help you move forward in faith?

Joshua, whose name means the LORD saves, appears quietly in Ephraim's genealogy, later leading Israel into the promised land, foreshadowing Jesus who bears his name. Where in your life do you need to trust Jesus, our greater Joshua, to lead you into the rest and hope He promises?

Even scattered, mostly forgotten tribes are folded honestly into Israel's family record here. How does knowing you belong to God's larger family, even when your own story feels small or overlooked, shape how you face this week?
